The facts, as stated in the petition, are that the proceeding land measuring 7.37 acres, appertaining to OS Jote No. 87/231 and RS Khatian 967 No. 39 and RS Plot No. 967 and 967/1530 originally belonged to Peta Ali who died leaving no heirs except his wife, Amir Bibi, who became the owner of the land and subsequently sold the land to the first party No. 1 petitioner, Sayedur Rahman, and his brother Abul Hossain in 1924 by Registered Kabalas. Sayedur Rahman and Abul Hossain then got their names mutated in CS Khatian and other Government records. Since the purchase they have been in possession of the said land but in Bangladesh Survey the second party fraudulently got their names recorded which was later on corrected by the first party by a petition under section 30 SAT Act. First party No. 2 petitioner, Abdul Jabbar, subsequently purchased the entire share of Abul Hossain from the heirs of late Abul Hossain and 3½ kanis from 1st party Sayedur Rahman by registered kabalas in 1976 and 1977. Since then the petitioner Abdul Jabbar has been in peaceful possession of the proceeding land by paying rent and taxes and by giving borga of the proceeding land. 

 10. The learned Magistrate in the instant case has therefore to decide whether any or each of the parties at the date of the order was in possession of the disputed land. A serutiny of the judgment of the learned Magistrate shows that he had unfortunately proceeded more on the basis of certain documentary evidence like CS, RS,. DP Khatians, certain judgments and orders, Kabuliats, rent receipts, etc, adduced by both the parties and had given elaborate discussion on title and interest instead of finding out the possession of either parties. Even then, it appears that he was not sure which parties had the title. In the process he had side tracked the main question and had failed to come to a categorical finding on the question of who was in possession at the relevant time. Whatever little attempt he made to find out which party was in possession is again marred by contradiction and vacillation in his judgment. At times he said that the first party was in possession of the disputed land while at other times he had stated that the second party was in possession.
